intro: Ives’s scherzo draws on Hawthorne’s fantastic stories rather than narrating one plot. Rapid figuration, quiet clusters, ragtime, hymn and march change the piano’s behaviour as abruptly as a scene changes in a story.
question: What holds a movement together when its musical scenes keep interrupting one another?

cues.title: A scherzo of changing scenes
cues.text: The opening throws rapid piano figures into a sharply accented texture. Rather than waiting for a regular scherzo tune and trio, listen for changes of musical behaviour: this movement assembles contrasting scenes from Hawthorne’s fantastic world.
cues.evidence: Gann describes the opening arpeggios and the movement’s collage design: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: the opening rises rapidly in level, with dense detected attacks at 0:25–0:40. Ives calls the movement a scherzo in his Introduction: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3673/pg3673-images.html#intro .
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rapid motion, uneven weight
cues.text: In the opening rush, activity and emphasis do not move in a perfectly even stream. Follow the sharper attacks within the running texture; an accent can redirect attention without bringing the motion to a complete halt.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: dense 0:25–0:45 activity, a strong boundary at 0:44 and a local drop at 0:50 before renewed force. This describes the measured contrast, not an inferred beat pattern. Opening texture: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: A cluster need not shout
cues.text: The first quiet episode changes the piano from rapid motion to sustained colour. Ives’s score uses a felt-covered board for soft clusters of neighbouring black keys above a slower melody: a cluster can form a background rather than a crash.
cues.evidence: Gann describes the first slow episode’s fifteen-inch felt-covered board, upper black-key clusters and melody beneath: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . The report’s 1:10 boundary and sustained drop in level and attack density support the approximate episode location; the recording does not document Liang’s physical implement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Not Hawthorne’s whole moral world
cues.text: Ives’s Hawthorne essay discusses guilt and the Puritan conscience, then says that this fundamental side of the novelist is not what his movement attempts. He chooses the wilder, childlike and fantastic stories instead.
cues.evidence: Ives, Essays Before a Sonata, “Hawthorne”, final two paragraphs: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3673/pg3673-images.html#hawthorne .

cues.title: Quiet does not mean empty
cues.text: Through the quieter episode, distinguish a melody from the colour surrounding it. Soft dissonance can remain in the background while a line proceeds at a different pace; the contrast with the opening depends on that separation as well as on loudness.
cues.evidence: Gann’s description of melody beneath quiet clusters supplies the listening distinction: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . The report shows sparse attacks through much of 1:15–2:35, interrupted by a local rise at 2:15; no uninterrupted soft dynamic or exact note is claimed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Ragtime as a verb
cues.text: In the busy stretches, listen for accents that seem to pull against a regular beat. Ives uses ragtime less as a fixed song form than as a way of displacing accents and making familiar material behave unpredictably.
cues.evidence: Gann discusses Ives’s use of “rag” as a verb and his interest in syncopation: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . The report anchors a broad increase in activity after 2:35, especially 3:10–3:55; it does not measure syncopation or locate a specific offbeat at 3:00.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The convenient road to heaven
cues.text: Hawthorne’s 1843 satire The Celestial Rail-Road turns Bunyan’s difficult pilgrimage into a comfortable train ride. Ives draws on it without following its plot continuously; the railway belongs among several literary images, not a timetable for every passage.
cues.evidence: Gann explains Hawthorne’s parody and Ives’s non-linear treatment, citing a 1913 memo: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . Ives names “Celestial Railroad” among numerous possibilities: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3673/pg3673-images.html#hawthorne .

cues.title: Activity sustains the paragraph
cues.text: This busy stretch keeps its force across successive gestures. Listen for the way sharp attacks form a continuous argument even when the melodic surface changes; not every new figure announces a new section.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: relatively high level and 2.2–3.6 detected attacks per second persist through 4:00–4:30, then level rises further at 4:35. No particular quotation is identified by these measurements. Collage and ragtime context: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: The interruption matters
cues.text: As the forceful paragraph subsides, listen for a change in the kind of attention the music asks for. The quieter statements are not merely the busy music played softly: their spacing makes the interruption itself part of the form.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: level falls from −7.6 dB at 4:50 to −34.6 at 5:00; no attacks are detected in the 4:55 window. Gann describes hymn interruptions within ragtime activity: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: An outburst between quiet statements
cues.text: The quiet is broken by a brief, forceful return of activity, then reasserts itself. Hear the contrast as an interruption in both directions: the busy music can cut into the hymn-like stillness just as stillness can interrupt the rush.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: −39.3 dB at 5:05 rises to −5.4 at 5:20, then drops to −30.5 at 5:30; strong boundaries at 5:14 and 5:30. Gann identifies the alternation of rag material and quiet Martyn quotations: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: A hymn against the circus
cues.text: Ives’s essay imagines an old hymn that protects the churchyard from a circus parade’s secular noise. Gann identifies the movement’s quiet hymn as Martyn, associated with “Jesus, lover of my soul”; his reading of it as the railway’s pilgrims remains an interpretation.
cues.evidence: Ives’s hymn/circus image: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3673/pg3673-images.html#hawthorne . Gann names Martyn and explicitly introduces the pilgrims reading as his own: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: A firmer tread
cues.text: After the quiet interruptions, the music regains weight and a more public, march-like manner. Compare a firm underlying tread with the displaced accents of ragtime; both belong to Ives’s store of vernacular music, but they organise motion differently.
cues.evidence: Gann places a march after the hymn-interrupted rag sequence: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . The report shows a strong restart at 6:16–6:22 and sustained high activity through 7:05. Placement is passage-level; machine onset estimates do not identify the march’s beats.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A pause does not conclude
cues.text: A short reduction in activity opens a gap, but the piano immediately rebuilds. Listen for the restart as a new direction inside the movement, not a final cadence waiting for applause.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: −24.3 dB and 0.2 detected attacks per second at 7:10 give way to −8.6 dB and 3.2 at 7:20. Gann describes the march slowing to a pause before renewed ragtime: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: Drum parts on a keyboard
cues.text: Ives recalled his father finding him playing the town band’s drum parts on the piano with his fists. In Jan Swafford’s account, George responded by sending him for drum lessons. It is a remembered childhood story, not a record of this performance’s technique.
cues.evidence: Swafford explicitly presents the episode as a story told by Ives: https://charlesives.org/ives-man-his-life . Gann connects the movement’s later fist clusters with pianistic imitation of drums: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: Accumulation before the break
cues.text: The late ragtime span gathers density and force. Listen for the piano acting increasingly as percussion as well as a carrier of tunes; the score’s fist clusters enlarge that contrast between pitched line and massed impact.
cues.evidence: Gann places a fist-cluster climax at the end of the long renewed ragtime section: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . The report shows dense 8:20–8:50 activity, including 4.8 attacks per second at 8:25 and a loud crest at 8:45; it does not establish the pianist’s hand position.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: After the impact
cues.text: The accumulated force collapses into a much quieter restart. Let the sudden space register before searching for the next tune: the size of this break changes how the following fragments are heard.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: strong boundary at 8:56; level falls from −5.6 dB at 8:45 to −44.5 at 9:00, with very sparse attacks at 8:55. Gann describes the restart after the cluster climax: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: A tune assembled from fragments
cues.text: In the later part, phrases of Columbia, the Gem of the Ocean become progressively more recognisable. Listen for identity arriving by accumulation: Ives can develop a tune before letting it sound complete, reversing the usual order of theme and variation.
cues.evidence: Gann describes the late Columbia material and cites J. Peter Burkholder’s term “cumulative form”: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . The report anchors a restart after 8:56 and a renewed rise at 9:32–9:45, but does not identify the tune’s first notes.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: How something happens
cues.text: Ives lists frost on a window, Feathertop, The Seven Vagabonds and Phoebe’s garden among possible associations. His qualification is precise: “not something that happens, but the way something happens”. The music need not assign one story to every scene.
cues.evidence: Ives, Essays Before a Sonata, final paragraph of “Hawthorne”: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3673/pg3673-images.html#hawthorne .

cues.title: A dip inside the build
cues.text: Even near the end, the busy texture briefly loses weight before renewing its force. Track the larger accumulation across that dip; a local easing does not necessarily announce the movement’s final withdrawal.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: −7.1 dB at 10:40 drops to −20.2 at 10:45, then rises to −6.8 at 10:55. Gann describes the late accumulation leading into complex rapid figuration: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: Keep one fragment in view
cues.text: Through the final rapid figuration, try retaining one recognisable shape while other notes move around it. The texture does not require every passing figure to be a new theme; familiar scraps can persist inside a much denser field of motion.
cues.evidence: Gann describes a late “whirlwind” of triplet figures with recognisable motives passing through it: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . The report supports dense late activity from 11:05, often four or more detected attacks per second; no single motif is aligned here.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The rush has staying power
cues.text: The final busy span continues rather than immediately dissolving. Listen for how sustained activity delays the close: the movement can keep changing its surface while preserving the pressure of the passage.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: high activity and level persist from 11:35 through 12:20, including 5.2 detected attacks per second at 11:45 and 4.8 at 12:00. Late-form context: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: The last interruption
cues.text: The rush finally gives way to quiet, but a small final gesture remains before the sound disappears. Listen past the withdrawal instead of treating the first fall in level as the ending.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: level falls sharply at 12:25–12:30, rises locally at 12:35, then reaches −60.5 dB at 12:40 within the 762.4-second file. Gann describes a last reminiscence and closing joke: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

transitions.title: Rapid figures become sustained colour
transitions.how: The opening’s rapid figuration gives way to a slow episode in which a melody lies beneath quiet upper-register clusters. The score’s neighbouring black keys create a sustained colour rather than an ordinary supporting triad. A change in density and pace, not a conventional cadential preparation, separates the two musical scenes; dissonance remains even though the manner of playing is softer.
transitions.evidence: Gann describes the first slow cluster episode: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: boundary at 1:10; level drops from −8.3 dB at 1:05 to −31.1 at 1:25, with sparse attacks. The written technique is not evidence of Liang’s particular implement.

transitions.title: Sustained colour yields to accented motion
transitions.how: The quiet episode releases its sustained colour into more forceful, accented motion. In the score’s ragtime writing, displaced accents disturb the relation between a beat and its emphasis; the piano changes from holding a background to projecting successive gestures. The join is a contrast of activity and touch, not a claim that the harmony suddenly becomes simpler.
transitions.evidence: Gann identifies a fast rag after the quiet cluster episode: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: level and attacks rise strongly between 2:30 and 2:40, followed by further active bursts. The 2:38 boundary is approximate; onset density is not a measured beat.

transitions.title: The busy paragraph admits another voice
transitions.how: Quiet hymn material interrupts the ragtime rather than emerging as its smoothly extended phrase. The piano’s reduced weight and wider spacing make the change of idiom audible. Ives then lets the busy music break back in, so the join is not a permanent replacement: two kinds of music can make competing claims within one passage.
transitions.evidence: Gann identifies two quiet Martyn interruptions in the rag material: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: major boundary at 5:00 after the 4:55 drop; renewed force at 5:15–5:20 and another deep drop at 5:30 support the alternation.

transitions.title: A quiet statement gives way to tread
transitions.how: The quiet interjections yield to renewed activity and a march-like tread. A more regular underlying motion offers a different kind of organisation from the ragtime’s displaced accents, while the piano retains the force of a public, outdoor musical idiom. The march is itself temporary: it slows to a pause before the longer ragtime accumulation resumes.
transitions.evidence: Gann’s sequence is interrupted ragtime, march, pause, renewed ragtime: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: boundaries at 6:16 and 6:22, large level rise by 6:20 and sustained activity until a 7:10 dip. The exact march downbeat is not established.

transitions.title: Accumulated force is abruptly removed
transitions.how: The later ragtime accumulation culminates in the score’s fist clusters, then the piano restarts slowly and quietly. There is no need for a dominant pedal to announce the new paragraph: the removal of weight and the sudden space between attacks provide the boundary. Fragments in the lower part will gradually make the patriotic tune more recognisable.
transitions.evidence: Gann supplies the cluster climax and subsequent cumulative Columbia material: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: 8:56 boundary after −5.6 dB at 8:45; −42.0 at 8:55 and −44.5 at 9:00. No exact physical technique is inferred from the recording.

transitions.title: The quiet restart begins to gather weight
transitions.how: The sparse restart does not remain a separate slow interlude. Its gestures gain weight and activity, drawing the listener into another accumulation. In the larger passage, fragments of Columbia, the Gem of the Ocean become more recognisable; the map marks the audible rebuilding, not the precise first appearance of that tune.
transitions.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: boundary at 9:32; level rises from −22.3 dB at 9:30 to −9.3 at 9:45 with more attacks. Gann describes cumulative recognition in this later region: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

transitions.title: Separate gestures become a continuous rush
transitions.how: The later accumulation passes into sustained rapid figuration. Recognisable motives need not disappear, but their fragments travel inside a busier surface rather than standing alone. The score’s complex triplet figures increase the sense of continuous motion; the final quiet interruption will therefore cut across an established rush rather than merely finish an already fading phrase.
transitions.evidence: Gann describes the late triplet-time whirlwind: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . cache/analysis/ives-concord-hawthorne.txt: attack density rises from 2.2–2.4 at 10:55–11:00 to around 4.0 from 11:05, remaining high through much of the ending. The map does not claim an aligned first triplet.

facts: With his father George Ives in Danbury; composition with Horatio Parker at Yale, 1894–98
Church organist until 1902; New York insurance business, ultimately Ives & Myrick
The Concord Sonata and Essays Before a Sonata at his own expense; 114 Songs, 1922
American hymn tunes · marches · ragtime · Beethoven · Emerson and Thoreau
composer.background:
Charles Ives grew up in Danbury, Connecticut, where his father George directed bands, played the cornet and taught music. George had served as a Union bandmaster during the American Civil War. The son’s later recollections describe experiments with bands playing different tunes, quarter-tone instruments and singing in one key against an accompaniment in another. These accounts are filtered through a son’s memory of his father, but the musical questions they pose recur in the scores: how far apart can independent parts move before they stop making a perceptible whole?

Ives was also trained in conventional musicianship. He became a paid church organist as a teenager and wrote the organ Variations on America in 1891. At Yale, from 1894 to 1898, Horatio Parker taught him counterpoint, orchestration and large-scale form. His First Symphony belongs to that apprenticeship, with audible debts to European symphonic writing. George died in 1894, shortly after Charles entered Yale. The practical musical culture of Danbury subsequently became both a source of material and a standard against which Ives judged the professional concert world.
composer.epithet: A church organist and insurance executive who made hymns, marching bands and incompatible tempos coexist inside concert music.
